content: To improve patient literacy, empower individuals and communities, and redefine patient-centered care to mitigate the emergence and spread of drug-resistant viruses, the following best practices are recommended: 1. HIV Drug Resistance (HIVDR) Testing: There is a lack of comprehensive reports on the most sensitive, cost-effective, and actionable HIVDR testing methods, particularly for implementation in lowand middle-income countries. Efforts should focus on defining and optimizing these methods. 2. Data Management for Next-Generation Sequencing: A standardized and simplified approach to managing data from next-generation sequencing outputs should be developed to facilitate its use in resource-limited settings. 3. Point-of-Care Tools for Drug Resistance: Simplified, evidence-based tools should be created and validated to interpret clinically relevant drug resistance mutations. These tools should be designed for use at the point of care. 4. Integrated Testing Approaches: The feasibility of affordable, simple public health-oriented tests that combine viral load and HIVDR testing should be explored. These tests should accommodate various specimen types, such as dried blood spots, dried plasma spots, and whole blood, and be deployable at or near the point of care to support decentralized healthcare delivery. 5. Drug Level Testing: These tests could guide decisions on whether HIVDR genotypic testing is necessary, particularly for identifying individuals who are non-adherent to antiretroviral therapy (ART). Public Health Response to Pretreatment HIV Drug Resistance (HIVDR) The prevalence of pretreatment HIVDR must be assessed comprehensively and nationally to understand its impact on ART program performance and resistance minimization. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed a framework to guide surveillance of acquired HIVDR in individuals experiencing ART failure. This includes population-level viral load suppression assessments and early-warning indicators to predict and address HIVDR. Preventing HIVDR is a critical component of global and national strategies. WHO’s Global Action Plan on HIV Drug Resistance (2017–2021) emphasizes the use of validated early-warning indicators to monitor resistance drivers at the clinic level. These indicators assess ART adherence, retention rates, viral load testing coverage, viral suppression levels, drug stock-outs, and timely switches to second-line ART when necessary. Annual monitoring of these indicators provides insights into ART clinic and program performance, enabling the identification of gaps in patient care, behavior, and program management. This information supports targeted interventions to improve service delivery. Dissemination and Updating of Guidelines WHO guidelines on public health responses to pretreatment HIVDR will be disseminated in print and electronically in English and French. The web version will include all annexes and supporting documentation. Member States will receive assistance in adapting the guidelines to their national contexts. An evaluation framework has been developed to assess the uptake of the guidelines and identify barriers to effective implementation. This policy analysis will inform the appropriateness of the guidelines within the context of the 2016 WHO consolidated antiretroviral (ARV) guidelines. WHO is committed to ongoing monitoring of viral load suppression and HIVDR prevalence at the population level to evaluate the impact on health outcomes. As new evidence emerges, supplements to the guidelines will be developed and incorporated into updates of the 2016 consolidated ARV guidelines. The introduction of new ARV drugs in first-line ART regimens is anticipated to influence the need for and type of responses required to address HIVDR. These considerations will be included in the next update of the WHO consolidated ARV guidelines, planned for 2019. Commitment to HIVDR Management WHO is dedicated to measuring, preventing, and mitigating the effects of HIVDR on treatment outcomes through country support, surveillance protocols, and guidance on HIVDR prevention and program strengthening. These efforts will be adapted as new evidence becomes available from epidemiological, intervention effectiveness, and implementation studies.
